subject: bandit2arm function for the analysis of Pavlovian learning task

messages.author: 922777ee1e270abd
messages.subject: bandit2arm function for the analysis of Pavlovian learning task
parts:
Hi,

I really appreciate your work and hope that the package will be further developed!
I'm a newbie to computational modelling and so my question is not very technical but more conceptual. But I hope you can still help me to figure it out.
I would like to apply bandit2arm_delta function to a classical rather then instrumental paradigm. In our task in each trial participants see on a screen one of two possible cues(blue or yellow) which is followed by presentation of a reinforcer (either unpleasent or neutral picture). The reinforcement scheme is 80%, by which I mean that for example after a yellow cue they have 80% chance to see an unpleasent picture and 20% chance to see a neutral one. The task is to predict (during cue presentation) what will happen - unpleasent or neutral picture (choice). 
I'm confused about interpretation of such choice and outcome. Should the choice still be coded as 1 (unpleasent) and 2 (neutral) while outcome as 1 (for any unpleasent event) and 0 for any other (neutral). Or maybe the outcome 1 should mean the correct guess (result consistent with the expectation) and 0 (or -1?) meaning no consistency between the expectation and result?
From the literature I know that the Rescorla-Wagner rule is used for clacssical conditioning, but I have trouble to translate it form instrumental learning, where people have a real choice, to Pavlovian learning, where the response does not impact on the outcome.
I actually tried analyzing my data in a way I described above (choice: 1-unpleasent, 2-neutral; outcome: 1-unpleasent, 0 - neutral) but the alpha rate was extremaly close to 0 for all participants, which suggests no learning. Now I'm wondering wheter my interpretation of data was wrong or they actually didn't learn. Also, I'm not sure if I need inverse temperature parameter here.

I'll be happy to with any suggestions!
Thank you,
Emilia
